Anthony Bourdain’s Life Doesn’t Sizzle In “Tony”

by Hunter Friesen, Contributor
Published August 19, 2026
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 6:39
Instaread

During the waning days of the press tour for “The Odyssey,” Christopher Nolan gave a surprisingly in-depth and frank interview with Chinese podcast host Zhong Shu. As part of their discussion, Nolan expressed one of his annoyances with modern film criticism: the tendency to gamify the experience of watching a film. Many viewers have an insecure need to stay one step ahead of the story, as if knowing what will happen before it happens is the mark of an intelligent audience member. And if we’re smarter than the movie, then the movie hasn’t pulled off its trick of illusion.

“Because to be able to identify the mechanism does not invalidate the mechanism…” he said. “Because people have this idea that, ‘Because I can understand why the story affects me the way it is, therefore, it didn’t work.’”

Apart from maybe superhero films, Nolan’s grievance finds its greatest home in the biopic genre. Whether it’s because they’re (somewhat) based on true stories with rigid parameters for what can and can’t happen, or simply because the formula sells lots of tickets, biopics have some of the most recurring and recognizable traits in all of cinema.

Throughout my time as a film critic, I’ve written ad nauseam about films like “I Wanna Dance with Somebody,” “Back to Black,” “Bob Marley: One Love” and “Bohemian Rhapsody.” Just as they all presented the same cadence of trials and tribulations for their central figures, I wrote the same critique about having to sit through the formula again and again. Perhaps my fixation on the routine story beats prevented me from digging deeper into the juicier thematic material.

Of course, as with Nolan’s view, my critique of those subpar films was not based solely on the fact that they followed the formula. Plenty of great biopics have followed the Rosetta Stone just as closely, including “A Complete Unknown,” “The Aviator” and Nolan’s own best picture winner, “Oppenheimer.”

What creates a feast out of a famine is the combination of every facet of the production. “Bob Marley: One Love” and “A Complete Unknown” both feature transformative performances — Kingsley Ben-Adir and Timothée Chalamet, respectively — at the center of their conventional stories. But only the latter featured the craft and unspoken warmth that kept me fully invested.

That brings us to “Tony,” the origin story of Anthony Bourdain — going by Tony here — before he became the bad boy of the culinary world through his book “Kitchen Confidential” and travel shows. Granted, he was always a bad boy, as evidenced by the opening quote, also prominently featured on the film’s poster: “I was — to be frank — a spoiled, miserable, narcissistic, self-destructive and thoughtless young lout.”

In his eyes, that roguish charm comes from cool wordplay and lies spun with such swagger that he believes everyone hangs on his every word like it is gospel. That’s why he tells everyone he’s going to get a summer writing fellowship grant from Vassar only a few minutes after leaving the interview.

It’s no coincidence that the two people who see right through him are women: his stern mother, Gladys (Dagmara Domińczyk), and Nancy (Emilia Jones), an older classmate he has a crush on. Unfortunately, the script by director Matt Johnson, Todd Bartels, Lou Howe and Matthew Miller does not support these women as anything beyond functions for Tony to become Anthony Bourdain. They are uninterested in him when the story needs him at his lowest, then interested once the story requires it.

The double whammy of their initial disinterest sets Tony on his course of self-discovery. Inevitably, he doesn’t get the writing fellowship. Instead of admitting that to his parents and friends, he steals all the cash from his dad’s wallet and hops on a bus. His destination is the seaside town of Provincetown, where he plans to repair his broken ego by wooing Nancy at her summer job.

On his first night in town, he’s thrown out of a restaurant for drunkenness, loses all his cash and ends up on the street. The restaurant’s owner and head chef (Antonio Banderas), who simply goes by Chef, takes pity on Tony and gives him a dishwasher job in exchange for the couple of bucks he needs to get home.

In the kitchen, Tony meets the salt and brine of the working class, filled with cursing, inappropriate jokes about coworkers’ mothers and the high stakes of surviving a lunch rush during the height of tourist season. It’s put up or shut up, with Tony unable to talk his way out of his inadequacy.

As he did a few years ago with “BlackBerry,” Johnson has crafted an ode to outcasts — those who sweat over a hot stove all day, then throw away their aprons to sit around a fire on the beach while throwing back a few (too many) beers. There’s a rambunctious rhythm to the kitchen’s chaos, the staff’s mismatched personalities merging into a found family.

It’s admirable that Johnson focused most of his efforts on that aspect because the biopic-y nature of this story is rather shallow, overrelying on our already established understanding of Bourdain. The spark that ignites his interest in cooking is largely absent, with only a handful of scenes featuring meals being served. For a movie about a chef, there was not a moment when my mouth watered, nor did I learn much about how a master chef begins his journey.

What I did connect with was Dominic Sessa’s lead performance, a natural extension of his revelatory debut in “The Holdovers” a few years ago. It’s Tony’s time to come of age, to figure out the person he truly is instead of the person he keeps telling everyone (and himself) he will become.

Banderas is also quite incredible in a role that could have used just a little more padding. Chef has found his oasis in the desert, secure enough in his dreams and ambitions to extend a helping hand to Tony, whose greatest life lesson comes from getting punched in the face while being thrown out on that first night.

Even when you think you can’t eat anymore, a great chef will bring out something that makes your stomach find a new level of appetite. Even with a talent like Johnson, “Tony” didn’t do that for me. It’s more or less another course in the endless meal that is the biopic genre. It’s appetizing to look at and has a smooth flavor, but little nutritional value.

A24 released “Tony” in select theaters Aug. 7. The film will expand nationwide Aug. 21.
